newsitem.title: USA: Wall St, tourists boost NYC, but job growth slows.
newsitem.headline: Wall St, tourists boost NYC, but job growth slows.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller said Thursday that New York City's economy was boosted by Wall Street's profits and a rising number of tourists, but warned job growth was slowing.

H. Carl McCall also cautioned that the city cannot count on financial markets staying strong and fattening the profits at banks and brokerage houses which in turn make big contributions to New York City's tax coffers.

"While the bright side of the local economic picture continues to be defined by the bull market on Wall Street, over the long term we need to be concerned about job growth and the financial markets' volatility," McCall said in prepared remarks.

New York City's personal inome was expected to rise 6.6 percent this year. During the first half, the city's personal income tax collections rose 8.0 percent, with estimated payments, which reflect capital gains as well as other sorts of income, climbed 10 percent. And corporate and business income taxes jumped 22 percent. McCall noted that both New York City's and New York State's budget surpluses stem from strong wage and income growth achieved by city workers.

But McCall also found a considerable decline in middle-class jobs, and little indication there will be enough jobs for former welfare recipients and job-seekers. New York City's labor force rose at nearly three times the U.S. rate this year but employment only grew half as fast.

"The city added only 3,100 jobs in the second quarter of 1997, compared with 15,400 jobs in the first quarter of the year," McCall said, noting the city's jobless rate was 10 percent. While strength in financial and tourism sectors buoyed real estate, professional and business services, retail sales and other consumer-driven industries, the state comptroller found a dramatic slowdown in job growth for culture and media in the city and around the nation.

Looking at all of the state, McCall found that the downstate area captured most of the new jobs, as upstate regions saw much slower consumption spending and a disturbing rise in household bankruptcies.

Saying the state could not just rely on Wall Street to fuel growth, McCall noted the four largest upstate areas--Albany, Buffalo, Rochester and Syracuse--only saw employment rise 0.4 percent in the first half. Long Island, which had a 1.4 percent rate of job growth, matching the city, appeared to benefit from its proximity to Wall Street. So did Long Island, where job growth climbed 1.2 percent.
